prompt: All three dimensions of a rectangular prism are doubled. The volume of the new prism is how many times the volume of the original?
hint: Volume multiplies three lengths together, and each one doubled.

hints.text: Volume multiplies three lengths together, and each one doubled.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a unit cube: a $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cube has volume $1$; doubled to $2 \times 2 \times 2$ it has volume $8$. Each of the three dimensions contributes one factor of $2$.

learningObjective: Apply the cube relationship between linear scale and volume.
explanation: Volume is $\ell wh$. Doubling each of the three dimensions gives $(2\ell)(2w)(2h) = 8\ell wh$.
So the volume becomes $8$ times as large.
Concretely: a $2 \times 3 \times 4$ prism has volume $24$; doubled to $4 \times 6 \times 8$ it has volume $192 = 8 \times 24$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: The 1, 2, 3 rule
steps: Scaling lengths by $k$ multiplies lengths by $k$, areas by $k^2$, and volumes by $k^3$.
The exponent is just the number of dimensions being measured.
Doubling gives $\times 2$, $\times 4$, $\times 8$ — and the trap answer is always the one that scaled linearly.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: 2 and 4 — the length and area answers — flank the correct 8 in the choices.
Volume is three-dimensional, so the factor applies three times: 2³. Match the exponent to the dimension being measured, always.
